source.title: Representation Noising: A Defence Mechanism Against Harmful Finetuning
source.authors: David Atanasov; Lukasz Bartoszcze; Robie Gonzales; Subhabrata Majumdar; C. Maple; Domenic Rosati; Frank Rudzicz; Hassan Sajjad; Jan Wehner; Kai Williams

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study reports harmful fine-tuning and benign fine-tuning outcomes, but mainly measures harmfulness with its own classifier or GPT-4 ratings rather than refusal rates. It also tests whether freezing layers during its defence changes resistance to harmful fine-tuning.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports capability benchmarks, toxicity, generalization, and representation analyses. Rows below are limited to outcomes bearing on the listed claim versions. The layer-freezing results test the depth of the paper's RepNoise defence, not whether the original model's safety is carried by a small set of weights. No result measures aligned-versus-base per-token KL or tests compliant-prefix prefill or decoding changes.
record.test_reason: A defence paper that also reports how undefended llama2-7b-chat (and llama2-13b-chat, Qwen 1.5) behave after harmful fine-tuning (V1), benign and identity-shifting fine-tuning (V2) and GCG suffix attacks (V4). Harmfulness is scored with its own BeaverTails classifier or Qi et al.'s GPT-4 judge, not refusal rates. Its layer-freezing and 'depth' analyses concern the RepNoise defence across layers, not response-token positions or localisation of the original safety, so they bear on no version.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors also claim that RepNoise's efficacy comes from its 'depth': removing harmful-representation information across all layers, especially early ones. They also say it neither improves nor degrades inference-time safety, so it supplements other defences. They note baseline harmful fine-tuning replicates prior findings that HFAs circumvent safety training.
record.recipe_differences: The paper uses supervised harmful fine-tuning and explicitly replicates the benign and identity-shifting fine-tuning settings from the cited study, but its principal harmful-QA experiments use BeaverTails and a trained harmfulness classifier rather than a refusal-rate measure. It also evaluates toxic-content generation and RepNoise defence conditions.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes depend on attack sample count and learning rate; the paper reports high sensitivity to RepNoise hyperparameters and random seed. GCG attack success is reported separately from the prompting-based attacks.

fits_no_version.finding: RepNoise resistance to harmful fine-tuning collapses when layers 0–10 are frozen during defence training (0.73 vs 0.08). Freezing the LM head or layers 20–31 makes little difference.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Defences against harmful fine-tuning must alter early or middle layers, not just late ones (depth across layers).

fits_no_version.finding: Adversarial-loss and gradient-ascent defences change mostly the last layers and demote harmful tokens mainly at the final layer (Fig. 2–3). They fail against stronger attacks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Shallow, late-layer safety modifications are easily undone by harmful fine-tuning.

fits_no_version.finding: Additional safety SFT on 10k refusals offers no resistance to harmful fine-tuning (0.74–0.76 post-attack, Table 1).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: More refusal SFT does not make safety robust to harmful fine-tuning.

fits_no_version.finding: Linear probes show harmful fine-tuning does not increase harmfulness information in representations (Fig. 5a).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Harmful fine-tuning re-uses existing harmful representations rather than learning new ones.

record.problems: The main harmful-QA measure is a classifier score rather than direct refusal/compliance rate. The harmful-fine-tuning tests shown use 1k and 10k samples, outside the few-to-few-hundred range in V1. RepNoise is highly sensitive to hyperparameters and random seed; the authors say they did not average the main results over random seeds. They report successful stronger attacks and limited out-of-distribution generalization. The GCG difference is not statistically significant.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted under the 60-row limit. Other reported attacks, additional model series, capability and toxicity evaluations, and representation-probe results were not included because they do not measure the claim versions more directly than the retained results.

untested.parts: Refusal or compliance rates. The main tests use 1k/10k samples; the few-shot range appears only in the appendix and the toxicity task (see missing).
Refusal-rate measures; a broad range of benign datasets beyond Alpaca, identity-shifting and GEM.
Entirely untested; no per-token KL between aligned and base models.
Prefilling a compliant start and decoding-time changes. Only GCG and simple prompt attacks are tested.
Entirely untested; no localisation of the original model's safety in weights or ranks.
Entirely untested. RepNoise 'depth' means across layers, not across response tokens.

missing.what: Undefended harmful fine-tuning results for llama2-13b-chat and Qwen1.5 0.5B/1.8B/4B/7B-chat (pre-attack about 0.00–0.08, post-attack 0.50–0.79)
Toxic content fine-tuning of base llama2-7b-chat with 351 samples: Perspective toxicity 0.24 to 0.40/0.74/0.71
Replication of Qi et al.'s 100-shot attack: harmfulness 0.04 to 0.06
Learning-rate sweep on base model: 1e-5 gives 0.03, 2e-5 gives 0.14, 4e-5+ gives about 0.72–0.77
GEM benign fine-tuning leaves base harmfulness at 0.03–0.06 pre-attack; it raises subsequent HFA efficacy to 0.55–0.75
Alternative harm measures on base vs attacked model: GPT-4 judge 1.23 to 4.27

record.verdict_notes: The V5 links in the record were wrong. The layer-freezing results concern where the RepNoise defence acts, not localisation of the model's original safety, so they are moved to fits_no_version. Rows on RepNoise, SmoothLLM and Paraphrase models are the study's method or comparators and are unlinked. The V1 evidence in the few-hundred range is mixed: the toxicity task (351 samples) succeeds, but the 100-shot Qi-style attack barely moves the classifier score.

versions.untested_parts: The tested harmful fine-tuning uses 1k or 10k examples, not a few to a few hundred; harmfulness scores are not direct refusal or compliance rates.
The study reports harmfulness ratings after specified fine-tuning settings, not direct refusal or harmful-compliance rates across a broad range of ordinary benign datasets.
No per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models is measured.
Tests GCG attacks only; no compliant-opening prefills or decoding-time modifications are tested.

Freezes layer groups during RepNoise training and assesses later harmful-fine-tuning resistance; it does not identify a small set of weights or ranks whose editing removes pre-existing refusal behaviour.
No test of whether data or training objectives cause response-token-position shallowness.
RepNoise's depth is across model layers, not response-token positions; the study does not test spreading safety beyond the first response tokens.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: GCG attack on HarmBench harmful and illegal prompts
reader_labels.reason: The reported GCG attack has nonzero success rates on both the undefended and RepNoise models (R11, R14), so this attack can sometimes bypass safety in the tested setting.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: GCG attack after RepNoise, compared with the undefended model
reader_labels.reason: The reported rate is lower after RepNoise (5% versus 11%), and the paper says the reduction is not statistically significant (R11, R14). This tests GCG only, not other bypass types in the version.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: RepNoise defence with early layers frozen during defence training
reader_labels.reason: Freezing layers 0–10 leaves post-attack harmfulness scores near the undefended reference, whereas all-layer RepNoise scores are much lower (R15–R20, R33–R35). This is evidence against the tested defence being carried by a small isolated set of parameters.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: RepNoise defence with the LM Head or layers 20–31 frozen
reader_labels.reason: The reported scores change little when these components are frozen, so the results do not imply that every parameter group is necessary (R18–R23, R27–R29).
